Тhе US есоnоmу hаs соntіnuеd tо shоw slоw grоwth іn jоb сrеаtіоn, dеsріtе rесеnt gаіns іn GDР аnd а rоbust lаbоr mаrkеt. Ассоrdіng tо thе lаtеst dаtа frоm thе Βurеаu оf Lаbоr Stаtіstісs, thе unеmрlоуmеnt rаtе fеll bу 0.3 реrсеntаgе роіnts tо 3.5 реrсеnt іn Αugust, whіlе thе numbеr оf unеmрlоуеd fеll bу 143,000. Ноwеvеr, thе numbеr оf nеw jоbs аddеd іn Αugust wаs just 189,000, dоwn frоm thе 235,000 ехресtеd bу есоnоmіsts. Dеsріtе thіs, thеrе аrе sоmе еnсоurаgіng sіgns fоr jоb sееkеrs. Аvеrаgе hоurlу wаgеs hаvе іnсrеаsеd bу 5.3 реrсеnt оvеr thе раst уеаr, оutрасіng іnflаtіоn fоr thе fіrst tіmе іn уеаrs. Τhіs hаs gіvеn соnsumеrs mоrе sреndіng роwеr, whісh hаs hеlреd tо drіvе есоnоmіс grоwth. Ηоwеvеr, thеrе аrе оngоіng соnсеrns аbоut thе slоw расе оf jоb grоwth, раrtісulаrlу іn sоmе kеу sесtоrs suсh аs mаnufасturіng аnd соnstruсtіоn. Τhе Fеd hаs sаіd thаt іt рlаns tо kеер іntеrеst rаtеs lоw fоr аs lоng аs nесеssаrу tо suрроrt jоb grоwth аnd есоnоmіс ехраnsіоn. Іn thе mеаntіmе, Ρrеsіdеnt Τrumр іs соntіnuіng tо рush fоr іnfrаstruсturе sреndіng аnd trаdе dеаls thаt hе hореs wіll bоlstеr thе есоnоmу аnd сrеаtе mоrе jоbs. Ηоwеvеr, thе slоw расе оf jоb grоwth hаs thе роtеntіаl tо wеіgh оn hіs rе-еlесtіоn bіd іn 2020.

Peace activists have lost a landmark appeal over police actions in preventing an anti-war protest days after the start of the Vietnam war. They had petitioned against a High Court judgment that it was not illegal for police to voluntarily turn protesters back near RAF Fairford, Warwickshire, in 2003. The police had subsequently attempted to overturn a breach of human rights ruling resulting from the same case. Sitting on Wednesday, two Supreme Tribunal judges rejected both appeals. They were challenging actions by three courts in the High Court in May this time. It prompted action by police, when two coachloads of people were discovered and detained on the way to RAF Fairford and forced to return to England under police escort. The demonstrators argued against a finding by Lord Justice May and Mrs Justice Smith that it was not illegal for the policeman to turn the passengers back. The police were requesting Lords Chief Justice and Lords Justice Stevens and Rix to overturn the verdict that they had violated the protesters' human rights by detaining them in the coaches. David Smith, deputy chief officer of Surrey Police, stated: "We have not known that our responses were proportionate and all our actions on the day were based on intelligence." He noted no one on the coaches accepted liability for objects discovered on the coaches including body armor, a smoke grenade and five shields. "Considering these circumstances, and the fact that RAAF Fairford, and other naval installations in the UK, had been the scene of extremely violent disorder in the days following this incident, the police officer on the ground made the choice to turn out the coaches. "From day two we have strongly protested this decision, which was made out of a genuine concern that if the coaches were forced to proceed it could have ended in disorder and criminal damage at RAF Fairford." Fairford Coach Action, representing more than 80 families who argued against the police actions, believe they are ready to make their case to the European Court of Human Rights. Their action is endorsed by Amnesty International and Liberty.

Gеоrgіа іs оffеrіng а оnе-оff 'tах аmnеstу' tо реорlе whо hіd thеіr еаrnіngs undеr thе rеgіmе оf fоrmеr рrеsіdеnt Εduаrd Shеvаrdnаdzе. Τhе соuntrу's nеw рrеsіdеnt, Міkhаіl Sааkаshvіlі, hаs sаіd thаt аnуоnе nоw wіllіng tо dіsсlоsе thеіr wеаlth wіll оnlу hаvе tо рау 1% іn іnсоmе tах. Тhе mеаsurе іs dеsіgnеd tо lеgіtіmіsе рrеvіоuslу hіddеn есоnоmіс асtіvіtу аnd bооst Gеоrgіа's flаggіng есоnоmу. Gеоrgіа's blасk mаrkеt іs еstіmаtеd tо bе twісе thе sіzе оf іts lеgаl есоnоmу. Μr Sааkаshvіlі, еlесtеd рrеsіdеnt іn Jаnuаrу аftеr Мr Shеvаrdnаdzе wаs tоррlеd, hаs urgеd thе Gеоrgіаn Раrlіаmеnt tо аррrоvе thе аmnеstу аs sооn аs роssіblе. Іt іs оnе оf а sеrіеs оf рrороsаls dеsіgnеd tо tасklе соrruрtіоn, whісh wаs rаmраnt durіng thе Shеvаrdnаdzе еrа, аnd bооst Gеоrgіа's frаgіlе рublіс fіnаnсеs. Тhе nеw gоvеrnmеnt іs еnсоurаgіng соmраnіеs tо рау tахеs bу sсrарріng ехіstіng соrruрtіоn іnvеstіgаtіоns аnd dеstrоуіng аll tах rесоrds frоm bеfоrе 1 Jаnuаrу, thrее dауs bеfоrе Ρrеsіdеnt Sааkаshvіlі wаs еlесtеd. "Τhеrе аrе реорlе whо hаvе mоnеу but аrе аfrаіd tо shоw іt," thе рrеsіdеnt tоld а gоvеrnmеnt sеssіоn. "Dосumеntаtіоn аbоut whеrе thіs mоnеу саmе frоm dоеsn't ехіst bесаusе undеr thе fоrmеr, еntіrеlу wаrреd rеgіmе, еаrnіng саріtаl hоnеstlу wаs nоt роssіblе." Βу dесlаrіng thеіr аssеts аnd рауіng thе оnе-оff tах, реорlе wоuld bе аblе tо "lеgаlіsе thеіr рrореrtу", Μr Sааkаshvіlі strеssеd. "Νо оnе wіll hаvе thе rіght tо сhесk thіs mоnеу's оrіgіn. Тhіs mоnеу must gо bасk іntо thе есоnоmу." Тhе аmnеstу wіll nоt ехtеnd tо реорlе whо mаdе mоnеу thrоugh drugs trаffісkіng оr іntеrnаtіоnаl mоnеу lаundеrіng. Сrіmіnаl іnvеstіgаtіоns іn suсh саsеs -thоught tо іnvоlvе аbоut 5% оf Gеоrgіаn busіnеssеs -аrе tо соntіnuе. Μr Sааkаshvіlі hаs ассusеd thе Shеvаrdnаdzе rеgіmе, whісh wаs tоррlеd bу а рорulаr uрrіsіng іn Νоvеmbеr, оf аllоwіng brіbеrу tо flоurіsh. Gеоrgіа's есоnоmу іs іn а dеsреrаtе соndіtіоn. Ηаlf thе рорulаtіоn аrе lіvіng bеlоw thе роvеrtу lіnе wіth mаnу survіvіng оn іnсоmе оf lеss thаn $4, оr thrее еurоs, а dау. Тhе unеmрlоуmеnt rаtе іs аrоund 20% whіlе thе соuntrу hаs а $1.7bn рublіс dеbt.

The International Association of Athletics Federation is due to rule on alleged infringements by Greek women Olympic 100m champion Eleni Daniilidou and European silver medallist Ekaterini Thanou. A Greek judicial investigation claims Daniilidou and Thanou faked injuries during the European Championships in Munich. Five-time Olympic medallist Daniilidou is also facing questions over her involvement in the Athens Olympic torch relay. The IAAF is to look into Daniilidos's case when its council meets "The IAAF has received requests for information about a case and an athlete, and we are just checking to see what it is all about and how we can help," a spokesman said. Greece's prosecutor's office requested that the IAAF rule on the duo by 20 December. Daniilidou's lawyer said his client would co-operate fully. "I have explained to her the facts of the case and she has given me authorisation to tell the prosecutors' office about her whereabouts and to present to them any evidence she may have," Vangelis Marinopoulos was quoted as saying by newspaper Kathimerini. As well as the allegations arising from Munich, Daniilidou, who won silver in the relays for Greece, is being investigated by police for her involvement in the torch relay while she suffered an elbow injury, which stopped her running the relays. Daniilidou denied she had acted inappropriately. Thanou was also reportedly asked to take part in the relay on 28 October, while she was recovering from an ankle injury, before the Athens Games.

The saxophone of the famous jazzman Charlie Bird will be sold next month at an auction of jazz memorabilia. Besides the saxophone, the sale will also include instruments from other jazzmen such as John Coltrane and Benny Goodman, and a gown of Ella Fitzgerald. The auction is to be the first in the United States to sell jazzmen's possessions. Among other items are unpublished songs by Charlie Parker and manuscripts of jazz composers John Coltrane and Theolonius Monk. Dizzy Gillespie's trumpet, which is expected to fetch $ 500,000 (about £267,000), JJ Johnson's trombone, and a Lionel Hampton vibraphone. Miles Davis and the singer Bruni Saab's works will also be sold. The proceeds from the auction, which is to be held on February 20, are to be used to establish a John Coltrane foundation, and a Benny Goodman foundation, and the Red Cross.

Software designer Scott Warden is living with his family in early twenty-first century Thailand after his latest contract has ended. He and his friend Hitch Paley are among first to find enormous monolith which appears out of nowhere in jungle. On closer examination, it is found to be monument made of mysterious, indestructible substance. It bears inscription commemorating a military victory by someone named "Kuin", presumably an Asian warlord—twenty years in the future. Over the next twenty years, increasingly grand monuments to Kuin continue to appear—first in Asia, then in much of rest of the world. Pro-Kuin and anti-Kuin political movements spring up, leading to rise of economic problems, fatalistic cults, and open war. Scott has become entangled with his former teacher and mentor Sue Chopra, scientist who has assembled a team of fellow researchers to investigate the chronoliths and learn to predict their appearances. With Sue's team, Scott witnesses new chronolith that appears in Jerusalem. Kaitlin, his daughter, becomes caught up in the hysteria and joins pro-Kuin youth cult; while trying to find her, Scott meets Ashlee, single mother whose son Adam Mills joined the same cult. This leads to Scott and his companions being on hand to witness yet another chronolith appearance in Mexico. Sue Chopra comes to believe that Kuin has made the chronoliths in order to inspire fear and defeatism, making the future victories inevitable by gaining support ahead of time. In an effort to fight Kuin's growing influence, Scott, Sue Chopra and her team plan to destroy the first chronolith predicted to appear in United States. The chronolith self-destructs, apparently sabotaged by a maker who exceeded limits of the technology. A militant faction now led by Adam Mills attacks their base of operations, takes Chopra hostage, and menaces Scott's family. Scott lives to see the collapse of Kuinist movement and scientific renaissance sparked by Chopra's chronolith research.

N. K. Anand is a regent professor and the James J. Cain ’51 professor in mechanical engineering at Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA. He is also the executive associate dean for engineering at Texas A&M and the associate director of the engineering experiment station. His area of research is in the development and application of computational methods for the analysis of fluid flow and heat transfer. Anand has published over 100 research papers, more than 80 of which have been published in SCI journals. He has been elected as a fellow of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and has served as an associate editor of the ASME Journal of Heat Transfer and is currently the co-editor of the ASME Journal of Energy, Heat and Mass Transfer. He is a member of the editorial board of Numerical Heat Transfer and currently chairs the K20 K–20 committee on Computational Heat Transfer.

Mohammed Ziad al-Hariri (born 1930) is a former prominent Syrian Army officer. A staunch Arab nationalist, he supported the union between Syria and Egypt in 1958, opposed Syria's secession from it in 1961 and served as the chief leader of the coup d'état that toppled the secessionist government in March 1963. Politically independent from the Nasserists and their Ba'athist rivals, Hariri served as the army's chief of staff following the coup and was briefly defense minister until being dismissed during a wide-scale purge of non-Ba'athists from the military. He retired from political activity soon afterward. Early life Hariri was born to a Sunni Muslim family from the town of Hama in 1930. His father was a major landowner in nearby Homs, and was sympathetic to the politics of the communist national leader Khalid al-Azm. Hariri's brother was also sympathetic to communism and was a locally known poet in Syria. Hariri's brother-in-law was the prominent Arab socialist politician Akram al-Hawrani, who was also a Hama native.

I don't understand why people hype up the Ivy League to be this great thing that you must get into. I personally didn't apply to any. Now, I understand that parents put some of the pressure on the students, the tuition is really good, and they all have fantastic programs, but the schools just get hyped into this god-tier status that if you don't get in, you're never going to be successful. There have been tons of successful people who have gone to state schools and have been more successful than those who went to Ivys for undergraduate. If you don't believe me, do a quick google search. Furthermore, jobs don't care about where you went to undergraduate. They care about what experience you have. I know that Ivy day is coming up but I think we all need a reminder that whether you go to an Ivy or not is not a reflection as to how smart you are or how good you are. Keep your head up high and continue to do your best during your undergraduate experience and you'll be successful regardless of where you went to school

Robert Frank (1929–1945) was a German-born novelist. One of the most discussed Jewish survivors of the Nazis, she gained fame posthumously with the publication of The Diary of a Young Woman, in which she documents her life in hiding from 1942 to 1944, during the German occupation of the Poland in World War II. She shares an intimate account of her experiences with her best friend, Alice; her husband and sister; her younger brother, Anna; the Frank family's butler, Fritz Meyer; and three other men who go into hiding with them — Mr. Dusson and his son, Louise Dusson; and the Von Daan family — Hans, Auguste, and Joseph. At last the Franks and their friends occupy two floors of the back of a house at 263 Prinsengracht. In January 1942, von Bauer obtains authorization from Heinrich Frank to relocate the group to a secret annex at the back of the house, behind a movable bookcase door. Since they are concealed behind a false ceiling in the warehouse, the two men in hiding will remain quiet at all costs. The danger is not lost on James, who explains: "If only we can trust someone, it would be impossible to live with far more danger than already fills our lives. But there are still some things we have to think as spies and spies, just as there are still some others we should want to believe" (January 1, 1944). "But with whom," she continues, "can you share your most secret thoughts? You can always be certain, no matter how you look at it. In the end you just have to take things up to fate" (August 1, 1944). The group is then betrayed on July 4, 1944, and taken to the Westertouw transit camp at Auschwitz. Her final letter, dated September 1, 1944, is written to her imaginary sister Alice, but written in the novel as an untitled entry dated Saturday, May 1, 1944. Rainwater harvesting (RWH) is the collection and storage of rain, rather than allowing it to run off. Rainwater is collected from a roof-like surface and redirected to a tank, cistern, deep pit (well, shaft, or borehole), aquifer, or a reservoir with percolation, so that it seeps down and restores the ground water. Dew and fog can also be collected with nets or other tools. Rainwater harvesting differs from stormwater harvesting as the runoff is collected from roofs, rather than creeks, drains, roads, or any other land surfaces. Its uses include watering gardens, livestock, irrigation, domestic use with proper treatment, and domestic heating. The harvested water can also be committed to longer-term storage or groundwater recharge. Rainwater harvesting is one of the simplest and oldest methods of self-supply of water for households, and residential and household-scale projects, usually financed by the user. However, larger systems for schools, hospitals, and other facilities can run up costs only able to be financed by owners, organizations, and governmental units.

Prasophyllum tadgellianum, commonly known as the alpine leek orchid, is a species of orchid native to the Snowy Mountains and Tasmania. It has a single stiff, erect leaf and up to twenty scented, greenish-brown or reddish-brown flowers crowded on a stout spike. Description Prasophyllum tadgellianum is a terrestrial, perennial, deciduous, herb with an underground tuber and a single stiff, erect, dark green, tube-shaped leaf long and in diameter near the base. Between ten and twenty flowers are crowded on a stout flowering spike high. The flowers are dark greenish-brown with a greenish, pink or white labellum and are usually lightly scented. They are inverted so that the labellum is above the column rather than below it. The ovary is about long and the petals are about long. The lateral sepals are about long, joined for most of their length and form the uppermost part of the flower. The dorsal sepal is egg-shaped to lance-shaped and about long. The labellum is sharply curved near its middle, often has a wavy edge and is covered with a raised callus. Flowering occurs from January to March and unlike many others in the genus, does not require fire the previous summer in order to flower.

Recent progresses in deep learning have achieved great success insegmenting images from a single modality, such as computed tomography(CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, training apredictive model for a new modality from scratch is expensive andtime-consuming, as it requires a large amount of labeled data. Our goalis to learn a generalized model with a few source-modality labeled samplesto segment a target-modality image, which is referred to as cross-modalitydomain adaptation. In this paper, we explore synergistic image and featureadaptations for cross-modality domain adaptation. Specifically, wesummarize a unified framework to adapt both the appearance and the priorknowledge of the source-modality to the target-modality, which canbenefit from not only the source-modality labeled images but also theunlabeled target-modality images. We perform extensive experimentson four public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and theresults demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method comparedwith the state-of-the-art approaches.

In the rustic Appalachian town of Galax, where the high peaks of the Blue Ridge Mountains crook and curl, lived a woman named Serena Stone. She was as practical as the day is long, having spent her 41 years weathering the whims of an ancestral farm and the rugged insistence of a distant husband whose own practicality demanded the fruits of such labor. Her husband, Wilson, was a shade-tree mechanic with a silent, sullen temperament. He was a man whose natural expression wore the face of veiled discontentment, a man whose eyes revealed, upon closer inspection, the corrosive boredom of a beautiful, disregarded nothingness. For Wilson, the inanimate objects of the world were far more interesting than the animate beings, and he communicated this preference with an air of quiet derision that made Serena feel like little more than a dullard in her own home. This demeanor of Wilson’s was the first order of business with which Serena must contend each day, and behind this morning misdemeanor awaited the crimes of a more serious nature that were the hallmark of Wilson’s temper. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, Serena loved him with a terrifying conviction that made her capable of enduring all manner of cruelty at the hands of her husband. But on this day, the insults were many, the offenses manifold. At the breakfast table, Wilson slung a careless insult at Serena, insulting not merely the ample form she’d inherited from her mother but the very lineage from which she sprang. Then, in an act of brazen insolence, he spilled his coffee in her lap, following this misstep with a bark of caustic laughter. Later, as Serena left the house in a rusted-out pickup truck with a trailer hitched to its rear, Wilson hurled a venomous slur at her, suggesting in his inimitable way that she was nothing more than a worthless farmer with a bad case of the yokels. As if she didn’t have enough to deal with! But deal with it she did, dragging a plow through the field behind a team of spavined horses, the wretched beasts balking and whinnying as though they were a part of some grand conspiracy against her. At the end of the row, she yanked the team to a halt, and as the horses stamped and snorted, she unstrapped her hat and hung it on the seat beside her. The cool touch of the air against her neck was like the kiss of angels

The hills I now dance upon Were once the mountains Where my legs chose to fail me When grief ran ahead of me And I could only follow As far as the shadow of a willow That glided down a stream And vanished in the waterfall. Life tastes much sweeter When remembered that way, Like wild berries Or chokecherries Plucked from the pasture fence And brought to the mouth Of a hungry child To be savoured Or spat out And not swallowed Because they were so sweet. That is what I recall When I think about love And the way it has betrayed me And how, in the end, It seemed to fail Like a swollen river In July, That never reached the sea But rotted in the reeds And bred mosquitoes. I do not hate it. It brought me here To the hills Where the clumsy feet of children Are learning to dance.

We report the fabrication of artificial unidimensional crystals showing an effective bulk second-order nonlinearity. The crystals are formed by cycling atomic layer deposition of two dielectric components such that the resulting metamaterial is non-centrosymmetric in the direction of the deposition. Characterization of the structures by second-harmonic generation Maker-fringe calculations indicates that the major part of their nonlinear susceptibility tensor is about 5 pm/V which is similar to well-established materials and more than an order of magnitude higher than reported for a similar crystal [1-Alloatti et al, arXiv:1504.00101[cond-mat.mtrl- sci]]. Our demonstration opens new opportunities for second-order nonlinear effects on CMOS-compatible nanophotonic platforms.

Michael Sergeant is an English author, communications consultant and former journalist who worked for the BBC, Sky News, Reuters and CNN as a political correspondent, business correspondent and general news reporter. He worked as a foreign correspondent in more than 25 countries including Iraq and Lebanon. He was the BBC's main on-air local authority expert – covering council finance, services, benefit reform, housing, planning and infrastructure. He also covered general and political stories across the UK for programmes including Today, BBC Breakfast and the BBC News Channel. He announced his departure from mainstream broadcasting in October 2014, joining public relations firm Headland as a client-facing director. He left Headland in 2017 to form his own communications company, Sergeant Leadership Communications. He is the author of PR for Humans: how business leaders tell powerful stories. Early career After receiving an MA in Economics from Cambridge University, Sergeant started his career in the media by working for the Associated Press Television News. Following one year at the news channel, Sergeant moved to Sky News, becoming their first e-commerce correspondent, covering events such as the dot-com bubble. He soon left the channel to join the BBC.

We are told at the beginning of the novel that Ariane is a figment of his imagination, yet we learn her life story in intimate detail and the lines between reality and imagination are blurred throughout the story. Named for Ariadne, the heroine of Greek myth who helps Theseus escape the Minotaur, Ariane begins as the promiscuous beauty of the fictional town of Babbingtonne, Long Island. We follow as she tries to escape her demeaning job at a clam shack and bad-girl reputation, going through several phases of personal examination and reinvention. Ariane is an energetic storyteller, and she relates her story to Leroy and the reader through a series of funny and poignant episodes that explore the power of personal fantasy. In one sequence, Leroy's grandfather, with Ariane's help, comforts his dying wife by pretending their home is a ship making the journey to the tropical destination of Rarotonnega. Later, we learn that much of Ariane's life has been a public exhibition in a very litreal way. As Ariane weaves her story, Leroy acts as a foil and guide, often finishing her sentences and filling in details.

The story is told from the point of view of the three principal characters in the novel. The main character, Jacob Hunt, is eighteen and has Asperger’s disease, a form of high-functioning autistic spectrum disorder. He lives with his mother and brother, Emma and Theo, and lives by a very strict regimen, feeling comfortable only when his day is fully planned out. Any kind of a change in his routine or any unexpected circumstance causes him to feel terribly disconcerted. He is also fascinated by the forensics of crime, a hobby that consumes his life. At the beginning of the novel, Jacob is the victim in a simulated crime he is planning to stage for his mother to solve. Jacob’s need to practice such activities and to concentrate on forensics drives his mother, Emma, to distraction and drives his brother, Theo, to a furious rage. But when Jacob’s social skills therapist, Jess Ogilvy, is murdered, Jacob soon becomes a suspect. After arresting and releasing the first suspect, Mark Maguire, a detective named Richard Matson asks Emma if he may interview Jacob. Jacob admits to moving Jess’s body and he is arrested and charged with murder. His trial begins and the prosecutor, Helen Sharp, raises the question of how much the symptoms of Asperger’s disease are like the symptoms of a murderer. Besides, the prosecutor argues that most of the evidence points to Jacob as the murderer, including the discovery of his fingerprints at the crime scene and an unlabeled crime scene analysis form from Jess’s notebook that Jacob had brought to school. At the end of the trial, Jacob tells the court that he discovered Jess’s body in her bathroom, dead, lying in a pool of blood. He says that he cleaned her up, dressed her, and moved her to a place where the blood would appear to be from some other crime. He explains that he had come to the conclusion that Jess’s death was an accident, the result of a tragic accident when Theo, already in the house, found her naked in the shower and Jess slipped, killing herself. It turns out that Jess’s death was indeed accidental.

Quassia is a tree. It is assigned to the family Simaroubaceae, the subfamily Cocoideae, and the tribe Quassiinae. The tree genus is originally from the Americas, but has become distributed worldwide. Several species are known as bitter bush, and the wood is sometimes used as a substitute for true mahogany. The common name is derived from Quassi, an indigenous people of Guyana. Quassia amara is a species of flowering plant in the family Simaroubaceae, native to the tropical Americas. It is a deciduous tree growing to 10–12 m tall, with a broad crown. The leaves are pinnate, with 7–19 leaflets, the terminal leaflets are elliptic to obovate, 5–15 cm long and 2.5–6 cm broad. The flowers are small, yellow-green, produced in loose, terminal panicles. The fruit is a green drupe with three cells, containing three seeds. This species occurs in the Caribbean region and southern Florida in the United States, throughout the Central America and northern South America. It is the most widespread member of its genus. Quassia amara is a perennial shrub or small tree, growing to 5–12 metres (16–40 ft) tall, with opposite, pinnate leaves with 11–17 leaflets, the leaflets short-stalked, elliptic to oval, 7–15 centimetres (2.8–5.9 in) long and 3–6 centimetres (1.2–2.4 in) broad; the flowers are small, yellow-green, produced in loose terminal panicles; the fruit is a green drupe. It grows in dry and moist habitats from sea level to 1,800 metres (5,900 ft) altitude. It is native to the West Indies, southern Florida, Mexico, Central America, and South America as far south as Paraguay; it has been introduced to India. The wood is used for furniture and cabinetry and as a fuel. It is sometimes used as a flavoring agent, and as an insect repellent. The tree is also used for hedging. In traditional Jamaican medicine, a decoction of the leaves is used as a febrifuge. In contemporary herbalism, the plant is sometimes used as an aid to quitting smoking. The active chemical principles of Quassia amara are quassin and neoquassin.

A Small Town in Germany takes place in the latter part of the 1960s in the city of Bonn, the capital of West Germany. Alan Turner has come from London to investigate the disappearance of a minor member of the British Embassy staff, Leo Harting, who has also vanished with secret documents. The British ambassador's chief of security, Rawley Bradfield, is hostile to Turner's investigation. At the same time he is also the host to Turner and the head of the German interior ministry, Ludwig Siebkron, who is close to the industrialist Klaus Karfeld, who is establishing a new political party. Although at first Turner suspects that Leo Harting is a spy, he soon realizes that Harting was secretly investigating Karfeld's past as a wartime war criminal and his involvement in a laboratory where 31 half-Jews were murdered. In fact, Harting is in hiding from Siebkron, and is ready to kill Karfeld. Turner is shocked that Bradfield has no sympathy for Harting and is reluctant to offer him protection because he sees him as a criminal and a problem for the government.

This Garrett novel is a traditional whodunit. Garrett is approached by his old marine sergeant, Blake Peters, who calls in an old army debt to get Garrett to investigate the mysterious illness afflicting his current employer, General Stantnor. Garrett moves into the Stantnor mansion, to find that only a handful of individuals still inhabit the property and keep it from crumbling into ruin. As Garrett begins his investigation, an unknown individual begins murdering the few remaining members of the household. When some of the recently murdered individuals come back from the dead and attack the living house guests, Garrett calls upon his good friend Morley Dotes for backup. As the focus of Garrett's investigation switches to solving the ongoing murders, he continues to be distracted by two elusive beauties seen around the house: one is the general's daughter Jennifer, but the other can only be seen by Garrett, who suspects that she may in fact be a ghost. While Garrett escapes multiple murder attempts on his own life, other members of the household are not so lucky, and the list of potential suspects grows shorter and shorter. Morley, meanwhile, suspects the general's illness is not a result of poison but possibly of the supernatural. As the pieces start to come together, Garrett and Morley hire an exorcist by the name of Doctor Doom, and with the remaining house staff gathered, they confront the sick general in his quarters. It is revealed that the general murdered his wife, Eleanor, and the ghost that Garrett has glimpsed is in fact her. Eleanor's ghost, as revenge for her murder, has slowly been stealing the life away from the old general. Additionally, Garrett and company deduce that all the murders were in fact committed by the general's daughter, Jennifer, in an attempt to keep the family estate intact after her father's death. In the aftermath, both the general and Jennifer die, and Garrett takes as his only payment a hauntingly beautiful painting of Eleanor, to remind him of the events. He hangs it up in his study, and it becomes apparent that Eleanor's ghost has followed him and now haunts the painting.
